paper_b.title: Stochastic Backpropagation and Approximate Inference in Deep Generative Models (Rezende, Mohamed, Wierstra, 2014)

metadata.description: Canonical parallel rediscovery: both papers independently derive the reparameterization trick for training deep generative models with continuous latent variables via variational inference. Kingma & Welling call it the 'reparameterization trick' in the VAE; Rezende et al. call it 'Gaussian backpropagation' in the DLGM. The core mathematical insight is identical: express z = mu + sigma * epsilon to push gradients through stochastic layers. The papers differ in emphasis: VAE focuses on the auto-encoding interpretation and simplicity; DLGM provides deeper theoretical grounding via Bonnet's/Price's theorems and explores hierarchical (multi-layer) latent structure.

matches.explanation: Both define a deep latent variable generative model with neural-network-parameterized likelihood. VAE describes a single-layer latent model: $z \sim p(z)$, $x \sim p_\theta(x|z)$. DLGM generalizes to a hierarchy of $L$ layers of latent Gaussians: $z_L \sim N(0,I)$, $z_l | z_{l+1} \sim N(\mu_l(z_{l+1}), \sigma_l^2(z_{l+1}))$. The single-layer VAE is a special case of DLGM with $L=1$.

Both introduce a neural-network-parameterized approximate posterior (recognition/inference model) $q_\phi(z|x)$ that maps observations to Gaussian distributions over latent variables. The functional form is identical: output mean and (log-)variance via a neural network. DLGM extends to hierarchical recognition $q_\phi(z_l|x, z_{<l})$ but the base concept is the same.

Both derive the same ELBO (variational lower bound / variational free energy): $\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z)) \le \log p_\theta(x)$. VAE calls it the 'ELBO' or 'variational lower bound'; DLGM calls it the 'variational free energy'. Identical mathematical object.

THE core shared contribution. Both independently discover the same technique: write $z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon$ with $\epsilon \sim N(0,I)$, so that gradients w.r.t. $\phi$ (which determine $\mu, \sigma$) can be computed by standard backpropagation through the deterministic function $g_\phi(\epsilon, x)$. VAE calls it the 'reparameterization trick'; DLGM calls it 'Gaussian backpropagation'. Mathematically identical. DLGM additionally provides the general-distribution correction terms via Bonnet's/Price's theorems, which VAE does not need because it restricts to the Gaussian case.

VAE's SGVB estimator (the specific Monte Carlo estimator of the ELBO using reparameterized samples) is named and formalized as a standalone contribution. DLGM uses the same estimator implicitly but does not name it separately.
The AEVB algorithm (the full training procedure packaged as an algorithm) is a VAE-specific contribution. DLGM describes the same training loop but does not formalize it as a named algorithm.

Both specify Gaussian encoder/decoder architectures. VAE details the specific encoder outputting $(\mu, \log \sigma^2)$ and decoder (Bernoulli/Gaussian), with closed-form KL for Gaussian-vs-Gaussian. DLGM uses similar Gaussian recognition networks but focuses more on the hierarchical multi-layer case.
Both derive the ELBO as a lower bound on $\log p_\theta(x)$ with the gap being the KL between approximate and true posterior. Standard variational inference derivation.

Both state and prove that the reparameterization/Gaussian-backprop trick yields unbiased, low-variance gradient estimators for both generative and recognition parameters, enabling end-to-end training via SGD. This is the main theoretical result of both papers.

Bonnet's theorem (gradient w.r.t. mean equals expected gradient w.r.t. sample) provides a theoretical foundation for Gaussian backpropagation that VAE does not develop. VAE takes the reparameterization as a direct computational trick without invoking these classical results.
Price's theorem (gradient w.r.t. covariance equals half the expected Hessian) is another theoretical underpinning specific to DLGM's more general treatment. Not in VAE.

DLGM's mention of normalizing flows to enrich the variational family beyond Gaussians is a forward-looking contribution not present in the original VAE paper (later developed in Rezende & Mohamed 2015).
Both evaluate on MNIST generative modeling, reporting marginal likelihood bounds and demonstrating learned latent representations with smooth interpolation. Comparable results.

unmatched_paper_a_explanations.DP_VAE.6: AEVB algorithm formalized as a named procedure. DLGM describes equivalent training without a named algorithm.

unmatched_paper_b_explanations.LP_DLGM.2: Price's theorem for covariance derivatives. Not in VAE.
unmatched_paper_b_explanations.DP_DLGM.5: Normalizing flows mention for richer variational families. Not in original VAE.

summary: This is a canonical parallel rediscovery (PR). Both papers independently derive the same core insight: reparameterize Gaussian latent variables as z = mu + sigma * epsilon to enable backpropagation through stochastic layers, yielding low-variance gradient estimators for variational inference in deep generative models. The ELBO objective, recognition model architecture, reparameterization trick, and main training theorem are essentially identical between the papers. They differ in emphasis and depth: VAE (Kingma & Welling) is more concise and operational, packaging the contribution as the AEVB algorithm and SGVB estimator; DLGM (Rezende et al.) provides deeper theoretical grounding via Bonnet's and Price's theorems, explores multi-layer hierarchical latent structure, and foreshadows normalizing flows. The community has adopted VAE terminology (reparameterization trick, ELBO) while recognizing the simultaneous independent discovery.
